slides: Now let's find the area of a polygon. We don't have one simple formula to use for every shape here. But we know how to find a triangle's area: a side, times the height to that side, divided by two.

slides.say: We also know the special quadrilaterals, like the square, the rectangle and the trapezoid. For a general quadrilateral, we don't have one of those ready-made formulas. So there are two ways. We cut the polygon into shapes we know. Or we see it as a bigger shape, minus the pieces that are missing.
Let's start with an easy one. This pentagon looks like a house. Its bottom part is a square with side six. On top there's a triangle, and its height is four.
at: This pentagon looks like a house

slides.say: We draw one line, and we get two shapes we know. The square is six times six, thirty-six. The triangle is its base, six, times its height, four, divided by two. Six times four is twenty-four, and half of that is twelve.
at: The square is six times six

slides.say: So the area of the pentagon is thirty-six plus twelve, forty-eight.
Here's a hexagon shaped like the letter L. Its sides are horizontal or vertical. The bottom is ten long, and the left side is six high. The top is four long, and the short side on the right is three.
at: Here's a hexagon shaped like the letter L

slides.say: The first way is to cut it. One line across gives two rectangles. The bottom one is ten long and three high. Ten times three is thirty.
The top one is four long. Its height is the left side, six, minus the three we used. Six minus three is three. So it's four times three, twelve. Together, thirty plus twelve is forty-two.
The second way is a big shape minus the missing piece. Let's complete the hexagon to a rectangle, ten by six. Ten times six is sixty.
at: complete the hexagon to a rectangle

slides.say: The missing corner is ten minus four, six long, and it's three high. Six times three is eighteen. So the area is sixty minus eighteen, forty-two. The same answer.
So when a polygon has no formula, look for lines that cut it into shapes you know. Or close it into a big shape, and take away what's missing.
For two regular polygons, there's one cut we always use. The first one is the regular hexagon. Like in the first lesson, we cut it into six equilateral triangles.
at: The first one is the regular hexagon

slides.say: Remember the area of an equilateral triangle with side a. It's a squared, times root three, divided by four.
Let's take a hexagon with side four. One triangle is four squared, sixteen, times root three, divided by four. Sixteen divided by four is four. So one triangle is four root three.
at: So one triangle is four root three
So one triangle is four root three

slides.say: The hexagon has six triangles. Six times four root three is twenty-four root three. Careful here. Many students stop at one triangle. But four root three is only one sixth of the hexagon.

The second one is the regular octagon. We cut a rectangle off the top and the bottom, and off the two sides. So we get a square in the middle, four rectangles, and four small triangles in the corners.
at: The second one is the regular octagon

slides.say: Why is each corner triangle a right triangle? The octagon's angle is one hundred thirty-five. The rectangle takes ninety of it. One hundred thirty-five minus ninety is forty-five. So the triangle has two angles of forty-five, and the third one is ninety. It's a silver triangle, forty-five, forty-five, ninety.
at: The octagon's angle is one hundred thirty-five

slides.say: Let's take an octagon with side two. The square in the middle has side two, so its area is two times two, four.
The hypotenuse of each corner triangle is a side of the octagon, two. In a silver triangle, we go from the hypotenuse to a leg by dividing by root two. Two divided by root two is root two.
So the area of one triangle is root two times root two, divided by two. Root two times root two is two, and half of that is one. Four triangles make four.
That's exactly the square. Put the four triangles together and they fill the square, like a square cut by its two diagonals. This is true in every regular octagon.
Each rectangle is two long, and its width is the leg of a triangle, root two. So it's two root two. Four rectangles make eight root two.

So the octagon is four, plus four, plus eight root two. That's eight plus eight root two. Always cut the octagon like this, even when they ask for only a part of it. And I'll see you in the next video.
at: That's eight plus eight root two
